title: Sorting Three Groups
statement: Every entry of the integer array `nums` is `1`, `2` or `3`. One operation deletes a single element of `nums` (the remaining elements keep their order). Return the fewest operations needed so that what is left is in non-decreasing order.
notes:
## Intuition

Deleting as few elements as possible is the same as keeping a longest non-decreasing subsequence. With only three values, a kept sequence is "some 1s, then some 2s, then some 3s". Picture walking through `nums` while sitting in one of three groups: you may move from group 1 to 2 to 3, never back. In group `g` you keep elements equal to `g` and delete the rest. Trying every pair of switch points (the brute force) costs O(n³); tracking the best cost of each group as you go costs O(n).

## Approach

1. Keep `cost1`, `cost2`, `cost3`: the fewest deletions for the prefix seen so far if the walk is currently in group 1, 2 or 3. All start at 0.
2. For each `value`, compute the new costs from the old ones:
   - staying in group 1 needs the previous walk to be in group 1;
   - being in group 2 may come from group 1 or 2, so take the smaller;
   - being in group 3 may come from any group.
   Each adds 1 when `value` does not match the group (it must be deleted).
3. Store the three new costs together, since each one was computed from the old values.
4. The walk may end in any group, so return the smallest of the three.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 1, 3, 2, 1]`, costs written as `(cost1, cost2, cost3)`, starting at `(0, 0, 0)`.

- `2`: `(1, 0, 1)`: only group 2 keeps it.
- `1`: `(1, 1, 1)`: group 1 keeps it after its earlier deletion; groups 2 and 3 delete it.
- `3`: `(2, 2, 1)`: group 3 keeps it, coming from a cost-1 state.
- `2`: `(3, 2, 2)`: group 2 keeps it from `min(2, 2) = 2`.
- `1`: `(3, 3, 3)`.

The smallest final cost is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): constant work per element.
- Space: O(1): three running costs.

## Pitfalls

- Compute all three new costs before overwriting any; updating `cost1` first would corrupt `cost2`'s `min`.
- A group may be empty, so group 3 must be reachable straight from group 1.
- Return the minimum over all three groups: for `[1]` the walk is cheapest in group 1, and `cost3` alone would give 1 instead of 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cost1`, `cost2`, `cost3` | fewest deletions so far when the walk is in group 1, 2 or 3 |
| `value` | the current element |
| `next1`, `next2`, `next3` | the costs after handling `value` |

narration.2: Before any element, every group costs nothing.
narration.6: Process the elements from left to right.
narration.7: Group 1 can only follow group 1; delete value unless it is a 1.
narration.8: Group 2 may follow group 1 or group 2, so start from the cheaper one; delete value unless it is a 2.
narration.9: Group 3 may follow any group; delete value unless it is a 3.
narration.10: Commit the new costs only now, because all three were computed from the old values.
narration.14: The walk may stop in any group, so the answer is the cheapest of the three.
